_link.title: I can identify management strategies for ASD, ADHD, and dyslexia

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following is a management strategy for ASD?

options.text: Behavioural therapy and speech therapy
options.explanation: ASD can be managed through behavioural therapy, speech and occupational therapy, educational support, and medication for accompanying conditions.

options.text: Audio learning and text-to-speech technology
options.explanation: Audio learning and text-to-speech technology are management strategies for dyslexia, not ASD.

options.text: Decluttering and working in small increments
options.explanation: Decluttering and working in small increments are behavioural strategies for ADHD management.

options.text: Vision correction and hearing aids
options.explanation: Vision and hearing devices are not management strategies for ASD.

toLevel2.stem: Which behavioural strategy is used to manage ADHD in a classroom?

options.text: Working in small increments with short breaks
options.explanation: Working in small increments is a recognised behavioural strategy for managing ADHD.

options.text: Speech therapy to improve communication
options.explanation: Speech therapy is a management strategy for ASD, not ADHD.

options.text: Text-to-speech technology for reading tasks
options.explanation: Text-to-speech technology is a management strategy for dyslexia.

options.text: Occupational therapy for sensory processing
options.explanation: While occupational therapy can be used across conditions, it is primarily listed as a management strategy for ASD and dyslexia.

toLevel2.stem: Which management strategy is specifically associated with dyslexia?

options.text: Assistive text-to-speech technology
options.explanation: Text-to-speech technology helps bypass the reading difficulties associated with dyslexia.

options.text: Medication for hyperactivity
options.explanation: Medication for hyperactivity is a management strategy for ADHD.

options.text: Behavioural therapy for social skills
options.explanation: Social skills-focused behavioural therapy is more associated with ASD management.

options.text: Designating zones for organisation
options.explanation: Designating zones is a behavioural strategy for ADHD management.

toLevel2.stem: What types of therapy can be used to manage ASD?

options.text: Behavioural therapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy
options.explanation: These are the main therapeutic approaches used in ASD management.

options.text: Only medication with no therapy component
options.explanation: ASD management includes multiple therapy types; medication addresses accompanying conditions, not ASD itself.

options.text: Only educational support with no therapy
options.explanation: ASD management includes both educational support and various therapies.

options.text: Physical therapy and surgery
options.explanation: Physical therapy and surgery are not standard management approaches for ASD.

toLevel2.stem: When is management of neurodivergent conditions most effective?

options.text: When tailored to the individual and implemented as early as possible
options.explanation: Management is most effective when personalised and started early.

options.text: When the same strategy is applied to everyone
options.explanation: One-size-fits-all approaches are less effective; management should be tailored to the individual.

options.text: When delayed until adulthood
options.explanation: Early implementation of management strategies produces better outcomes.

options.text: When only one strategy is used at a time
options.explanation: Multiple strategies can be combined for more comprehensive support.

toLevel2.stem: ADHD can be managed through medication, counselling, and behavioural strategies such as decluttering, designating zones, using {{blank:1}}, and working in small {{blank:2}}.
Dyslexia can be managed through audio or video learning, assistive {{blank:1}} technology, and occupational {{blank:2}}.
ASD can be managed through behavioural therapy, {{blank:1}} therapy, occupational therapy, educational support, and medication for accompanying {{blank:2}} conditions.
Medication is used in ASD management to treat ASD itself directly.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is incorrect. Medication in ASD management is used for accompanying mental health conditions, not to treat ASD directly.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Correct. Medication is used to manage accompanying mental health conditions such as anxiety or depression, not ASD itself.

toLevel2.stem: Management strategies are most effective when tailored to the individual's specific profile.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. Personalised management that considers the individual's specific strengths and challenges produces better outcomes.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This is incorrect. Tailored, individualised management is more effective than one-size-fits-all approaches.

toLevel3.stem: Why does a student with ADHD benefit from decluttering their desk before starting a task?

options.text: Because removing unnecessary items reduces distractions and helps the student focus on the task at hand
options.explanation: Decluttering addresses the ADHD challenge of inattention by minimising competing stimuli.

options.text: Because a clean desk improves handwriting
options.explanation: The purpose is to reduce distraction, not to improve handwriting.

options.text: Because it is a punishment for not paying attention
options.explanation: Decluttering is a supportive strategy, not a punishment.

options.text: Because it forces the student to sit still
options.explanation: The purpose is to reduce visual distractions, not to control movement.

toLevel3.stem: How does text-to-speech technology address the specific challenges of dyslexia?

options.text: It converts written text to audio, bypassing the difficulty of converting written symbols to sounds
options.explanation: Text-to-speech directly addresses the core challenge of dyslexia by providing information in an auditory format.

options.text: It makes the text larger on the screen
options.explanation: Enlarging text addresses vision problems, not the symbol-to-sound processing difficulty in dyslexia.

options.text: It translates text into a different language
options.explanation: Translation does not address the symbol-to-sound processing challenge in dyslexia.

options.text: It removes all text from the screen
options.explanation: Removing text would remove access to information; the technology converts text to speech.

toLevel3.stem: Why is early implementation of management strategies important for neurodivergent conditions?

options.text: Because early support allows individuals to develop effective coping strategies and prevents secondary issues like low confidence
options.explanation: Early intervention supports development and prevents additional problems that can arise from unsupported challenges.

options.text: Because neurodivergent conditions disappear if treated early enough
options.explanation: Neurodivergent conditions are lifelong; early management improves functioning but does not eliminate the condition.

options.text: Because management strategies only work in childhood
options.explanation: Management strategies can be effective at any age, but early implementation provides the best outcomes.

options.text: Because early treatment is cheaper than later treatment
options.explanation: While cost may be a consideration, the primary reason is better developmental outcomes.

toLevel3.stem: Why is medication used alongside other therapies for ASD rather than as the sole treatment?

options.text: Because medication addresses accompanying conditions like anxiety but does not target the core features of ASD, which require therapeutic approaches
options.explanation: ASD management requires multiple approaches because medication alone does not address social communication or behavioural features.

options.text: Because medication for ASD has not been invented yet
options.explanation: Medication exists for conditions that accompany ASD; the point is that ASD itself requires therapeutic support.

options.text: Because medication is never effective for any condition
options.explanation: Medication can be effective for specific conditions; in ASD, it addresses accompanying issues rather than core features.

options.text: Because therapists require patients to also take medication
options.explanation: There is no requirement; the combination is based on clinical needs.

toLevel3.stem: How does using a visual planner help a student with ADHD during a maths lesson?

options.text: It provides external structure for tracking progress, compensating for internal difficulties with organisation and time management
options.explanation: Visual planners externalise organisation, which addresses the executive function challenges in ADHD.

options.text: It makes the maths problems easier to solve
options.explanation: The planner helps with organisation, not with the mathematical content itself.

options.text: It prevents the student from leaving their seat
options.explanation: The planner addresses organisation, not physical movement.

options.text: It replaces the need for a teacher
options.explanation: Visual planners supplement teaching; they do not replace teacher support.

toLevel3.stem: Why might audio or video learning be particularly effective for a student with dyslexia?

options.text: Because it provides information through auditory and visual channels, reducing reliance on the reading skills that are most challenged
options.explanation: Alternative learning formats play to dyslexia's strengths (strong memory, verbal comprehension) while bypassing reading challenges.

options.text: Because students with dyslexia cannot learn through any other method
options.explanation: Students with dyslexia can learn through multiple methods; audio/video is particularly effective but not the only option.

options.text: Because audio learning improves reading ability
options.explanation: Audio learning bypasses reading difficulties rather than improving reading skills.

options.text: Because video learning is more entertaining than reading
options.explanation: The effectiveness is based on matching the format to the individual's processing strengths, not entertainment value.

toLevel3.stem: Decluttering a student's desk helps manage ADHD by reducing {{blank:1}} that compete for the student's {{blank:2}}.
Text-to-speech technology converts {{blank:1}} text to audio, bypassing the {{blank:2}}-to-sound processing difficulty in dyslexia.
Medication in ASD management addresses accompanying conditions like {{blank:1}}, while the core features of ASD require {{blank:2}} approaches.
Working in small increments helps students with ADHD because it breaks tasks into manageable chunks that match their attention capacity.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. Small increments with breaks accommodate the attention regulation challenges in ADHD.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This is incorrect. Breaking tasks into smaller segments is an effective strategy because it works with, not against, ADHD attention patterns.

toLevel4.stem: A teacher has a student with ASD who becomes overwhelmed during unstructured group activities. Which management strategy would be most appropriate?

options.text: Providing clear structure, assigned roles, and predictable routines within the group activity
options.explanation: Structure and predictability address ASD-related challenges with unstructured social environments.

options.text: Removing the student from all group activities permanently
options.explanation: Exclusion does not manage the condition; adapted participation with support is more appropriate.

options.text: Providing text-to-speech technology
options.explanation: Text-to-speech is a dyslexia strategy; it does not address the social/structural challenges in ASD.

options.text: Asking the student to work faster to keep up with the group
options.explanation: Increasing pressure does not address the underlying challenge and may increase distress.

toLevel4.stem: A student with ADHD loses track of time during a maths exam and fails to finish. Which combination of strategies could help this student in future exams?

options.text: Using a visual timer, working through problems in small increments, and having a clear plan showing the number of questions to complete per section
options.explanation: These strategies address the time management and organisation challenges specific to ADHD.

options.text: Speech therapy and occupational therapy
options.explanation: These are ASD management strategies, not ADHD strategies for exam time management.

options.text: Audio learning and text-to-speech technology
options.explanation: These are dyslexia management strategies, not ADHD strategies.

options.text: Giving the student more homework to practice time management at home
options.explanation: More homework does not directly address the time management challenge during exams.

toLevel4.stem: A student with dyslexia is falling behind in a history class that relies heavily on reading primary source documents. Which management strategy would most effectively support this student?

options.text: Providing audio recordings of the documents or text-to-speech software so the student can access content through listening
options.explanation: Audio formats bypass the reading challenge while allowing the student to engage with the historical content.

options.text: Requiring the student to read the documents more slowly
options.explanation: Slower reading does not address the neurological processing difficulty.

options.text: Behavioural therapy to improve social skills
options.explanation: Social skills therapy is an ASD strategy, not relevant to the reading challenge.

options.text: Decluttering the student's desk
options.explanation: Decluttering is an ADHD strategy that does not address reading difficulties.

toLevel4.stem: A parent asks what they can do at home to support their child with ADHD. Which recommendation is most appropriate based on ADHD management strategies?

options.text: Create designated zones for different activities, use planners for homework, and break tasks into small steps with breaks
options.explanation: These are established ADHD management strategies that can be implemented in a home environment.

options.text: Provide speech therapy exercises at home
options.explanation: Speech therapy is primarily an ASD management strategy.

options.text: Install text-to-speech software on all devices
options.explanation: Text-to-speech is a dyslexia management strategy.

options.text: Remove all structure from the home to encourage independence
options.explanation: Removing structure is counterproductive; ADHD management involves providing external structure.

toLevel4.stem: A school has three students: one with ASD, one with ADHD, and one with dyslexia. The school wants to provide appropriate support for each. Which matching of strategy to student is correct?

options.text: ASD: occupational therapy and structured routines; ADHD: planners and small increments; Dyslexia: text-to-speech and audio learning
options.explanation: Each strategy matches the specific challenges of the corresponding condition.

options.text: ASD: text-to-speech; ADHD: speech therapy; Dyslexia: decluttering
options.explanation: These strategies are mismatched to the wrong conditions.

options.text: The same strategy should be used for all three students
options.explanation: Different conditions require different management strategies.

options.text: ASD: audio learning; ADHD: occupational therapy; Dyslexia: behavioural therapy
options.explanation: These strategies are not correctly matched to the conditions.

toLevel4.stem: A student with ASD is experiencing significant anxiety alongside their ASD features. How should the management approach address both?

options.text: Use therapeutic approaches like behavioural therapy for ASD features and consider medication to manage the accompanying anxiety
options.explanation: ASD management combines therapy for core features with medication for accompanying mental health conditions like anxiety.

options.text: Only treat the anxiety and ignore the ASD
options.explanation: Both the ASD features and the anxiety need to be addressed for comprehensive support.

options.text: Only use medication for both ASD and anxiety
options.explanation: Medication addresses anxiety but does not manage core ASD features, which require therapeutic approaches.

options.text: Use text-to-speech technology for both conditions
options.explanation: Text-to-speech is a dyslexia strategy and does not address ASD or anxiety.

toLevel4.stem: A workplace wants to support an employee with dyslexia who needs to read lengthy reports. Which management approach would be most effective?

options.text: Providing reports in audio format or providing text-to-speech software for the employee's computer
options.explanation: These dyslexia management strategies bypass reading difficulties while ensuring the employee can access the information.

options.text: Asking the employee to read the reports more carefully
options.explanation: Reading difficulty in dyslexia is neurological, not related to care or effort.

options.text: Providing a planner and designated work zones
options.explanation: These are ADHD management strategies, not dyslexia strategies.

options.text: Offering behavioural therapy sessions during work hours
options.explanation: Behavioural therapy is primarily an ASD management strategy and does not address dyslexia's reading challenges.

toLevel4.stem: For a student with ASD who becomes overwhelmed in unstructured activities, the most appropriate strategy is to provide clear {{blank:1}} and predictable {{blank:2}}.
A student with ADHD benefits from using a visual {{blank:1}} to track completed tasks and working in small {{blank:2}} with short breaks.
Matching management strategies to conditions: ASD uses {{blank:1}} therapy; ADHD uses decluttering and planners; dyslexia uses {{blank:2}} technology.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why a one-size-fits-all management approach is less effective than individualised strategies for neurodivergent conditions.

options.text: Because each condition has different neurological features requiring different strategies, and each individual within a condition has a unique profile of strengths and challenges
options.explanation: Variation exists both between conditions and between individuals with the same condition, making personalisation essential.

options.text: Because all neurodivergent individuals have the same needs
options.explanation: This is the assumption behind a one-size-fits-all approach, which is incorrect.

options.text: Because individualised strategies are only important for adults
options.explanation: Individualised strategies are important at all ages.

options.text: Because management strategies are never effective regardless of approach
options.explanation: Management strategies can be highly effective when properly tailored.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the potential unintended consequences of implementing ADHD management strategies (like decluttering and planners) for a student who actually has ASD.

options.text: The strategies may not address the student's actual challenges such as social communication difficulties and need for routine, potentially leaving them without effective support
options.explanation: Mismatched strategies fail to address the specific needs of the condition, wasting resources and leaving the student unsupported.

options.text: The strategies would work equally well because ASD and ADHD are the same condition
options.explanation: ASD and ADHD are different conditions requiring different management approaches.

options.text: The strategies would cause physical harm to the student
options.explanation: The strategies are unlikely to cause physical harm, but they would be ineffective for the wrong condition.

options.text: There would be no consequences because all strategies help all students
options.explanation: Mismatched strategies are ineffective and may leave genuine needs unaddressed.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse how management strategies for each of the three conditions (ASD, ADHD, dyslexia) reflect the specific neurological differences underlying each condition.

options.text: ASD strategies address social communication and sensory needs linked to cortex and amygdala differences; ADHD strategies address executive function linked to cerebral cortex delay; dyslexia strategies bypass symbol processing linked to language area differences
options.explanation: Each set of strategies is designed to address the specific neurological challenges of the respective condition.

options.text: Management strategies are chosen randomly and have no connection to neurology
options.explanation: Effective strategies are directly informed by the neurological basis of each condition.

options.text: All three conditions have the same neurological basis, so any strategy works for any condition
options.explanation: Each condition has distinct neurological features that require targeted strategies.

options.text: Only medication-based strategies reflect neurological differences
options.explanation: Non-medication strategies also reflect neurological understanding by addressing specific functional challenges.

toLevel5.stem: A school provides text-to-speech software for all students as a universal support measure. Evaluate whether this approach adequately addresses the management needs of students with ASD, ADHD, and dyslexia.

options.text: It primarily benefits students with dyslexia but does not address the specific needs of ASD (social communication, routine) or ADHD (organisation, attention), so it is insufficient as the sole measure
options.explanation: While text-to-speech is valuable for dyslexia, the other conditions require different management strategies.

options.text: It adequately addresses all three conditions because technology helps everyone
options.explanation: Different conditions have different needs; one technology cannot address all of them.

options.text: It is harmful to students with ASD and ADHD
options.explanation: It is not harmful, but it is insufficient for conditions that require different types of support.

options.text: It only benefits neurotypical students
options.explanation: Text-to-speech particularly benefits students with dyslexia, but does not replace other needed supports.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why occupational therapy appears as a management strategy for both ASD and dyslexia but serves different purposes in each condition.

options.text: For ASD, occupational therapy addresses sensory processing and daily living skills; for dyslexia, it addresses fine motor skills related to writing—the same therapy type targets different functional needs
options.explanation: Occupational therapy is adaptable and targets different goals depending on the condition's specific challenges.

options.text: Occupational therapy does exactly the same thing for both conditions
options.explanation: The therapy is tailored to the specific needs of each condition.

options.text: Occupational therapy is only effective for ASD, not dyslexia
options.explanation: It is listed as effective for both conditions, targeting different functional areas.

options.text: Occupational therapy is irrelevant to both conditions
options.explanation: It is a recognised management strategy for both ASD and dyslexia.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the importance of combining multiple management strategies rather than relying on a single approach for any one condition.

options.text: Multiple strategies address different aspects of functioning; for example, ADHD medication addresses neurochemistry while behavioural strategies address daily organisation, creating more comprehensive support
options.explanation: Each strategy targets a different facet of the condition, and combining them provides more complete support.

options.text: A single strategy is always sufficient if it is the right one
options.explanation: Neurodivergent conditions affect multiple areas of functioning, so a single strategy rarely addresses all needs.

options.text: Multiple strategies always conflict with each other
options.explanation: Strategies can complement each other when properly coordinated.

options.text: Combining strategies is only important for severe cases
options.explanation: Combined approaches benefit individuals across the spectrum of each condition.

toLevel5.stem: A student with comorbid ADHD and dyslexia needs management support. Evaluate the challenges of designing an effective support plan for this student.

options.text: The plan must address both attention/organisation challenges from ADHD and reading/writing challenges from dyslexia simultaneously, requiring integration of strategies from both conditions
options.explanation: Comorbid conditions require careful integration of strategies that address the distinct needs of each condition.

options.text: Only the more serious condition needs to be addressed
options.explanation: Both conditions need attention for the student to receive comprehensive support.

options.text: The same single strategy can address both conditions
options.explanation: Different conditions require different strategies, even when they coexist.

options.text: Comorbid conditions cannot be managed at all
options.explanation: Comorbid conditions can be managed with integrated, individualised planning.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse how the principle that 'management is most effective when implemented early' applies differently to ASD, ADHD, and dyslexia given their different developmental presentations.

options.text: ASD is often identified early through social communication delays, ADHD may become apparent when school demands increase, and dyslexia typically emerges when reading instruction begins—each has a different optimal window for early intervention
options.explanation: The conditions present at different developmental stages, meaning 'early' intervention differs in timing for each.

options.text: All three conditions are always identified at the same age
options.explanation: The conditions typically present at different developmental stages.

options.text: Early intervention only matters for ASD
options.explanation: Early intervention benefits all three conditions, though the timing of identification differs.

options.text: The timing of intervention is irrelevant for all three conditions
options.explanation: Timing matters; earlier implementation generally produces better outcomes for all three.

toLevel5.stem: A one-size-fits-all approach fails because variation exists both {{blank:1}} conditions and between individuals with the {{blank:2}} condition.
A student with comorbid ADHD and dyslexia needs strategies that address {{blank:1}} challenges from ADHD and reading challenges from {{blank:2}} simultaneously.
